That's what I love about street photography.

For me, outdoor photography is a higher art form than studio photography or even painting because the photographer is out there in the moment and doesn't have any control on the objects or events surrounding them. I also appreciate black and white photos much more than color ones, since they make it a little bit abstract and allow room for some imagination.

I believe the articles says they are negatives...different from undeveloped film, isn't it? We have lots of negatives (stored away) and those taken on good film should be good for decades.
But aren't they sensitive to the tiniest light leakages? Like a few photons a day over decades will expose the entire area?

The negatives are developed film...just not printed on paper. They can be stored the same way as old photographs....you keep them out of light and heat to prevent fading or warping, and should keep them in appropriate sleeves and containers. I would assume the negatives in the story were stored that way.

Undeveloped film is what you need to protect from being exposed to any light at all or it will completely lose the picture. It's a lot more volatile, and I seem to recall that it's only good for about a year. It needs to get developed into negatives to fix the picture in place (so to speak).
